**Module 1** · 45 min · [Open the slides for this module](01-javascript-slides.html)
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Learning objectives"}
- Use `const`, `let`, arrow functions, objects and arrays.
- Write a class with a constructor, use `this`, and extend another class.
- Import and export between files.
- Use the browser console as a REPL.
:::

## Your REPL is the browser

Open any web page, then the developer tools: `F12`, or `Cmd` + `Option` + `I` on a Mac. The **Console** tab is a JavaScript prompt, like the R console or a Python shell.

```js
> 2 + 2
4
> 'cold' + ' ' + 'chain'
'cold chain'
> Math.max(3, 9, 4)
9
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Keep a console open for this whole lesson and try every example. While your game is running with `npm run dev`, the console can also reach into it: `game.scene.getScene('Play')` gives you the running scene, and you can change things live.
:::

## Variables

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```r
speed <- 200
speed <- 250        # fine
name <- "researcher"
```
## Python
```python
speed = 200
speed = 250         # fine
name = "researcher"
```
## JavaScript
```js
let speed = 200;
speed = 250;              // fine: let can change
const name = 'researcher';
name = 'cart';            // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
```
:::

Use `const` by default and `let` when the value has to change. You'll see `var` in old code. Don't use it.

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
Semicolons at the end of lines are optional in JavaScript, but the course (and most Phaser code) uses them. Single and double quotes mean the same thing.
:::

## Equality, and nothing

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```r
x == 5
is.null(x)
is.na(x)
```
## Python
```python
x == 5
x is None
```
## JavaScript
```js
x === 5        // use three: no type conversion
x !== 5
x === null     // "deliberately empty"
x === undefined // "never set"
```
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`==` also exists, but it converts types first, so `'5' == 5` is `true`. Always use `===` and `!==`.

JavaScript has two kinds of nothing. `undefined` is what you get from a variable or property that was never set. `null` is what code returns on purpose to mean "no value". Two operators make them easy to handle, and you'll see both in *Cold Chain*:

```js
const floor = data.floor ?? 0;              // ?? : use 0 if data.floor is null or undefined
const speed = cart.getData('config')?.speed; // ?. : undefined instead of an error if config is missing
```
:::

## Strings

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```r
sprintf("Stored: %d / %d", stored, target)
glue::glue("Stored: {stored} / {target}")
```
## Python
```python
f"Stored: {stored} / {target}"
```
## JavaScript
```js
`Stored: ${stored} / ${target}`   // backticks, not quotes
```
:::

## Arrays

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```r
thaw <- c(10, 55, 80)
thaw[1]              # 10: R counts from 1
length(thaw)
thaw[thaw > 50]
thaw * 2
```
## Python
```python
thaw = [10, 55, 80]
thaw[0]              # 10
len(thaw)
[t for t in thaw if t > 50]
[t * 2 for t in thaw]
```
## JavaScript
```js
const thaw = [10, 55, 80];
thaw[0];                       // 10: counts from 0, like Python
thaw.length;
thaw.filter((t) => t > 50);    // [55, 80]
thaw.map((t) => t * 2);        // [20, 110, 160]
thaw.push(95);                 // add to the end (const arrays can still change inside)
```
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
There's no vectorised arithmetic: `thaw * 2` is `NaN`. Use `map`, `filter` and `forEach` instead of loops when you can, as you would with `purrr` or a list comprehension.
:::

## Objects

An object is a bag of named values, like a named list in R or a dict in Python. Phaser configs are objects.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```r
cart <- list(axis = "x", speed = 110)
cart$speed
cart$speed <- 120
```
## Python
```python
cart = {"axis": "x", "speed": 110}
cart["speed"]
cart["speed"] = 120
```
## JavaScript
```js
const cart = { axis: 'x', speed: 110 };
cart.speed;          // 110
cart.speed = 120;    // fine: const means "always this object", not "frozen"
const { axis, speed } = cart;   // unpack into two variables
```
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
That last line is **destructuring**. You'll see it everywhere in Phaser code: `const { width, height } = this.scale;` is short for `const width = this.scale.width; const height = this.scale.height;`.
:::

## Functions

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## R
```r
thaw_after <- function(seconds, rate = 7) {
  seconds * rate
}
```
## Python
```python
def thaw_after(seconds, rate=7):
    return seconds * rate
```
## JavaScript
```js
function thawAfter(seconds, rate = 7) {
  return seconds * rate;    // return is required
}
```
:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
The same function as an **arrow function**:

```js
const thawAfter = (seconds, rate = 7) => seconds * rate;
```

(In the console, give it a new name or reload the page first: a name can only be declared once.)

Arrow functions are the short form, and the one you'll use most, especially for little functions you pass to something else: `thaw.filter((t) => t > 50)`. With one expression and no braces, the value is returned for you. With braces, you need `return`.

JavaScript names use camelCase (`thawAfter`), not snake_case.
:::

## Loops and conditions

```js
for (const t of thaw) {
  if (t >= 100) {
    console.log('thawed');
  } else if (t >= 75) {
    console.log('warning');
  }
}

for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { /* i is 0, 1, 2 */ }

const label = carrying ? 'THAW' : 'GET SAMPLE';   // ifelse() in one line
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`for ... of` loops over the values of an array. (There's also `for ... in`, which loops over *keys*. You rarely want it.)
:::

## Classes

Every scene and every game object in Phaser is a class. A class is a template for objects that carry their own data and their own functions (**methods**).

```js
class Sample {
  constructor(id) {           // runs when you write `new Sample(...)`
    this.id = id;             // `this` is the object being made
    this.thaw = 0;
  }

  warm(seconds) {             // a method: no `function` keyword
    this.thaw += seconds * 7;
    return this.thaw >= 100;  // true if it thawed
  }
}

const s = new Sample('HCT116-rep1');
s.warm(10);   // false
s.thaw;       // 70
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
R has several class systems (S3, S4, R6); this is closest to R6. In Python it's an ordinary class, with `this` instead of `self`, and you don't list `this` as an argument.
:::

## Extending a class

`extends` makes a new class from an existing one. `super(...)` runs the parent's constructor, and has to come first.

```js
import Phaser from 'phaser';

export class Play extends Phaser.Scene {
  constructor() {
    super('Play');      // run Phaser.Scene's constructor, with the key 'Play'
  }

  create() {            // your version of a method Phaser.Scene already has
    this.add.text(16, 16, 'Hello');
  }
}
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
This is the shape of every scene in the course. `Phaser.Scene` already knows how to load files, run the loop and draw; you **extend** it and fill in `preload`, `create` and `update`. Because `Play` *is* a `Phaser.Scene`, `this` inside its methods has everything a scene has: `this.add`, `this.load`, `this.physics`, `this.scale`.
:::

## The one thing about `this`

Inside a method, `this` is the object. But a function you pass to someone else gets **their** `this`, not yours. Arrow functions are the exception: they keep the `this` of the place they were written.

```js
create() {
  this.stored = 0;

  this.time.delayedCall(1000, () => {
    this.stored += 1;     // arrow: `this` is still the scene ✓
  });

  this.time.delayedCall(1000, function () {
    this.stored += 1;     // regular function: `this` is something else ✗
  });
}
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
That's the whole rule, and it's the source of more beginner bugs than anything else in JavaScript. When you pass a function to Phaser, use an arrow function. When you pass a method (`this.pickUp`), Phaser usually lets you say what `this` should be as an extra argument, which is why lesson 4 has lines like:

```js
this.physics.add.overlap(this.player, this.sample, this.pickUp, null, this);
//                                                                   ^ `this` inside pickUp
```
:::

## Modules: one file, one job

Each file is a module. It **exports** what other files may use and **imports** what it needs.

```js
// src/save.js
export function loadBestTime() { /* ... */ }
export function saveBestTime(ms) { /* ... */ }
```

```js
// src/scenes/Results.js
import Phaser from 'phaser';                          // a package, from node_modules
import { loadBestTime, saveBestTime } from '../save.js'; // a file of yours: path, with .js
```

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`import Phaser from 'phaser'` takes the package's **default** export and calls it `Phaser`. The braces in `{ loadBestTime }` take **named** exports, by name. It's like `library()` and `from x import y`, except that every name is explicit, so you can always find where something came from.
:::

## npm and Vite

| | R | Python | JavaScript |
|---|---|---|---|
| Install packages | `install.packages()` | `pip install` | `npm install` |
| The project's dependencies | `DESCRIPTION`, `renv.lock` | `requirements.txt`, `pyproject.toml` | `package.json`, `package-lock.json` |
| Where packages go | your R library | `site-packages` | `node_modules/`, in the project |
| Run a project script | | | `npm run dev`, `npm run build` |

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}
`npm install` reads `package.json` and puts Phaser and Vite in `node_modules/`, inside the project. Every project has its own copy, a bit like an `renv` library. Never commit `node_modules/`.

**Vite** is the tool behind `npm run dev`. It serves your game to the browser, follows your `import`s, and reloads the page when you save a file. In lesson 10, `npm run build` uses it to bundle everything into a few files you can put on any web server.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Exercise 1.4: Spot the bug — the counter that never counts" .exercise #ex-1.4}
This scene should show "Stored: 1" after one second. It stays at "Stored: 0", and the console has no errors. Why?

```js
create() {
  this.stored = 0;
  this.label = this.add.text(16, 16, 'Stored: 0');

  this.time.delayedCall(1000, function () {
    this.stored += 1;
  });
}

update() {
  this.label.setText(`Stored: ${this.stored}`);
}
```

[Answer](../answers/01-javascript-answers.qmd#ex-1.4)
:::

## Key points

- `const` by default, `let` when it changes, never `var`. `===`, never `==`.
- Arrays count from 0. Use `map`, `filter` and `forEach`.
- Objects are named lists or dicts. Destructuring unpacks them: `const { width, height } = this.scale`.
- Every scene is a class that `extends Phaser.Scene`. `this` inside its methods is the scene.
- Pass arrow functions to Phaser, so `this` stays the scene.
- `import` and `export` connect files. `npm install` fills `node_modules/`, and Vite serves the game.
